title: “I Won’t!” Said Mary
paragraphs: There was so much to do in the garden that morning that Mary got back to the house late. She was in such a rush to return to her work that she forgot all about Colin until the very last minute.
“Tell Colin I can’t come to see him yet,” she said to Martha. “I’m very busy in the garden.”
Martha looked rather scared.
“Eh! Miss Mary,” she said, “it might put him in a terrible mood when I tell him that.”
But Mary was not as afraid of him as other people were, and she was not the kind of person who gave things up for others.
“I can’t stay,” she answered. “Dickon’s waiting for me.” And she ran off.

The afternoon was even lovelier and busier than the morning. Almost all the weeds were already cleared out of the garden, and most of the roses and trees had been trimmed or had the soil loosened around them. Dickon had brought a spade of his own and had taught Mary how to use all her tools. By now it was clear that the lovely, wild place would never become a neat “gardener’s garden,” but that it would be a wilderness full of growing things before spring was over.

“There’ll be apple blossoms and cherry blossoms overhead,” Dickon said, working away with all his strength. “And there’ll be peach and plum trees in bloom against the walls, and the grass’ll be a carpet of flowers.”

The little fox and the rook were as happy and busy as the children were, and the robin and his mate darted back and forth like tiny streaks of lightning. Sometimes the rook spread his black wings and sailed off over the treetops in the park. Each time he came back, he settled near Dickon and cawed a few times, as if he were telling about his adventures, and Dickon talked to him just as he had talked to the robin. Once, when Dickon was so busy that he did not answer right away, Soot flew onto his shoulder and gently pinched his ear with his big beak. When Mary wanted to rest for a while, Dickon sat down with her under a tree. Once he pulled his pipe out of his pocket and played its soft, strange little notes, and two squirrels appeared on the wall to look and listen.
“You’re a good bit stronger than you were,” Dickon said, watching her dig. “You’re starting to look different, for sure.”
Mary was glowing from the exercise and in high spirits.
“I’m getting fatter every day,” she said, quite triumphantly. “Mrs. Medlock will have to get me some bigger dresses. Martha says my hair is growing thicker. It isn’t so flat and stringy anymore.”
The sun was starting to set, sending deep golden rays slanting in under the trees, when they said goodbye.
“It’ll be fine tomorrow,” said Dickon. “I’ll be working by sunrise.”
“So will I,” said Mary.

She ran back to the house as fast as her feet could carry her. She wanted to tell Colin about Dickon’s fox cub and the rook, and about everything spring had been doing. She felt sure he would like to hear it. So it was not very pleasant, when she opened the door of her room, to find Martha standing there waiting for her with a gloomy face.
“What is the matter?” she asked. “What did Colin say when you told him I couldn’t come?”
“Eh!” said Martha, “I wish you’d gone. He nearly threw one of his tantrums. There’s been a fine fuss all afternoon just to keep him quiet. He kept watching the clock the whole time.”

Mary’s lips pressed tightly together. She was no more used to thinking about other people than Colin was, and she saw no reason why a bad-tempered boy should get in the way of the thing she liked best. She knew nothing about how sad it is for people who have been sick and nervous, and who don’t realize they can control their tempers and need not make everyone else sick and nervous too. When she had had a headache in India, she had done her best to make sure everybody else had a headache, or something just as bad. She felt she had been perfectly right to do so, but of course now she felt that Colin was completely wrong.

His sofa was empty when she walked into his room. He lay flat on his back in bed and kept his face turned away as she entered. That was a poor beginning, and Mary stalked over to his bedside, stiff and cold.
“Why didn’t you get up?” she said.

“I did get up this morning, when I thought you were coming,” he answered, without looking at her. “This afternoon I made them put me back in bed. My back hurt and my head hurt and I was tired. Why didn’t you come?”
“I was working in the garden with Dickon,” said Mary.
Colin frowned, then graciously agreed to look at her.
“I won’t let that boy come here if you go off and stay with him instead of coming to talk to me,” he said.
Mary flew into a terrible rage. She could get angry without making any noise at all. She just turned sour and stubborn and stopped caring what happened.
“If you send Dickon away, I’ll never come into this room again!” she shot back.
“You’ll have to, if I want you,” said Colin.
“I won’t!” said Mary.
“I’ll make you,” said Colin. “They’ll drag you in.”

“Will they, Mr. Rajah!” said Mary fiercely. “They can drag me in, but they can’t make me talk once they get me here. I’ll sit with my teeth clenched and never tell you one thing. I won’t even look at you. I’ll stare at the floor!”

What a lovely, agreeable pair they made as they glared at each other. If they had been two little boys from the street, they would have leaped at each other and had a rough-and-tumble fight. As it was, they did the next best thing.
“You are a selfish thing!” cried Colin.
“And what are you?” said Mary. “Selfish people always say that. To them, anyone who won’t do what they want is selfish. You’re worse than I am. You’re the most selfish boy I’ve ever seen.”
“I am not!” snapped Colin. “I’m not as selfish as your precious Dickon is! He keeps you playing in the dirt when he knows I’m all alone. He’s selfish, if you ask me!”
Mary’s eyes flashed with fury.
“He’s the nicest boy who ever lived!” she said. “He’s—he’s like an angel!” That might sound rather silly, but she did not care one bit.
“Some angel!” Colin sneered savagely. “He’s a common cottage boy from the moor!”
“He’s better than a common Rajah!” Mary shot back. “He’s a thousand times better!”

Because she was the stronger of the two, she was starting to get the better of him. The truth was that he had never had a fight with anyone like himself in his whole life. On the whole, it was rather good for him, though neither he nor Mary knew it. He turned his head on his pillow and shut his eyes, and a big tear squeezed out and rolled down his cheek. He was starting to feel pitiful and sorry for himself—and for no one else.
“I’m not as selfish as you, because I’m always sick, and I’m sure there’s a lump coming on my back,” he said. “And I’m going to die, besides.”
“You are not!” Mary contradicted him, without a bit of sympathy.
He opened his eyes wide with outrage. He had never heard anyone say such a thing before. He was furious and a little bit pleased all at once, if a person can be both at the same time.
“I’m not?” he cried. “I am! You know I am! Everybody says so.”

“Well, I don’t believe it!” said Mary bitterly. “You only say so to make people feel sorry for you. I think you’re proud of it. I just don’t believe it! Maybe it would be true if you were a nice boy—but you’re far too nasty!”
Despite his sickly back, Colin sat straight up in bed in a perfectly healthy rage.

“Get out of this room!” he shouted, and he grabbed his pillow and threw it at her. He was not strong enough to throw it far, and it only dropped at her feet, but Mary’s face looked as tight and sharp as a nutcracker.
“I’m going,” she said. “And I won’t come back!”
She walked to the door, and when she got there she turned around and spoke again.
“I had so many nice things to tell you,” she said. “Dickon brought along his fox and his rook, and I meant to tell you everything about them. Well, now you won’t hear a single word!”

She marched out the door and shut it behind her. There, to her great surprise, she found the trained nurse standing as if she had been listening, and, even more amazing, she was laughing. She was a big, handsome young woman who should never have been a trained nurse at all, since she could not stand sick people. She was always finding excuses to leave Colin to Martha or to anyone else who would take her place. Mary had never liked her. She just stood and stared up at her as the nurse stood giggling into her handkerchief.
“What are you laughing at?” she asked her.

“At you two youngsters,” said the nurse. “It’s the best thing that could happen to that sickly, pampered boy, to have someone stand up to him who’s as spoiled as he is.” And she laughed into her handkerchief again. “If he’d had a spitfire of a little sister to fight with, it would have been the saving of him.”
“Is he going to die?”
“I don’t know and I don’t care,” said the nurse. “Hysterics and temper are half of what ails him.”
“What are hysterics?” asked Mary.
“You’ll find out if you work him into another tantrum after this. But anyway, you’ve given him something to have hysterics about, and I’m glad of it.”

Mary went back to her room feeling nothing like the way she had felt when she came in from the garden. She was cross and disappointed, but not the least bit sorry for Colin. She had been looking forward to telling him many things, and she had meant to try to decide whether it would be safe to trust him with the great secret. She had been starting to think it would be, but now she had changed her mind completely. She would never tell him, and he could stay in his room and never get any fresh air and die if he liked! It would serve him right! She felt so sour and unforgiving that for a few minutes she almost forgot about Dickon, and the green veil creeping over the world, and the soft wind blowing down from the moor.

Martha was waiting for her, and the trouble on her face had been replaced, for the moment, by interest and curiosity. A wooden box sat on the table. Its lid had been taken off, and inside it was full of neat packages.
“Mr. Craven sent it to you,” said Martha. “It looks like it has picture books in it.”

Mary remembered what he had asked her the day she went to his room. “Do you want anything—dolls—toys—books?” She opened a package, wondering whether he had sent a doll, and wondering what she would do with it if he had. But he had not sent one. There were several beautiful books like the ones Colin had, and two of them were about gardens and full of pictures. There were two or three games, and there was a beautiful little writing case with a gold monogram on it, along with a gold pen and an inkstand.
The gifts were all so lovely that her delight began to crowd the anger out of her head. She had never expected him to remember her at all, and her stubborn little heart warmed up.
“I can write better than I can print,” she said, “and the first thing I’ll write with that pen will be a letter to tell him I’m very grateful.”

If she had been friends with Colin, she would have run straight to show him her presents. They would have looked at the pictures, read some of the gardening books, and maybe tried the games. He would have enjoyed himself so much that he would never once have thought about dying, or put his hand on his spine to feel for a lump. He had a habit of doing that, and she could not stand it. It gave her an uncomfortable, frightened feeling, because he always looked so frightened himself. He said that if he ever felt even a small lump, he would know his hunch had begun to grow. He had gotten the idea from something he had heard Mrs. Medlock whispering to the nurse, and he had thought about it in secret until it was firmly fixed in his mind. Mrs. Medlock had said that his father’s back had started to show its crookedness that way when he was a child. Colin had never told anyone but Mary that most of his “tantrums,” as people called them, grew out of this hidden, hysterical fear. Mary had felt sorry for him when he told her.
“He always starts thinking about it when he’s cross or tired,” she said to herself. “And he’s been cross today. Maybe—maybe he’s been thinking about it all afternoon.”
She stood still, looking down at the carpet and thinking.

“I said I would never go back again—” she hesitated, knitting her brows—“but maybe, just maybe, I’ll go and see him—if he wants me—in the morning. Maybe he’ll try to throw his pillow at me again, but—I think—I’ll go.”
